subject: Automotive & EVs
title: The Steering Column Problem
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Steering Column Problem.

hook.text: Early steering columns were solid steel rods aimed directly at the driver's chest.

buildup.text: In a head-on crash, the driver slid forward and was impaled on the rigid column.

discovery.text: Béla Barényi proposed a collapsible column that would crumple harmlessly on impact.

twist.text: Automakers resisted the idea for decades, calling it too expensive and unnecessary.

climax.text: After Ralph Nader exposed car dangers in 1965, collapsible columns became mandatory.

punchline.text: A column built to break on purpose saves the driver.

quiz.question: What did Béla Barényi propose for steering columns?

details.summary: Early steering columns were rigid steel shafts that impaled drivers during frontal crashes. Collapsible steering columns, introduced in the 1960s, compress on impact to prevent this deadly outcome.
details.whyItMatters: The rigid steering column was one of the deadliest features of early cars. Collapsible designs eliminated a major cause of driver chest and head fatalities in frontal collisions.
takeaways: Rigid columns acted like spears aimed at the driver's chest
Collapsible columns telescope on impact to absorb energy
GM introduced the first collapsible column in 1967 models

faq.question: How does a collapsible steering column actually work?
faq.answer: The column is built from nested tubes or a mesh section that crushes progressively during impact. Some designs also incorporate a breakaway bracket that allows the column to move away from the driver.

faq.question: Was the steering column the leading cause of driver death before the fix?
faq.answer: Yes. In frontal crashes the steering column was responsible for a large portion of fatal chest injuries. The combination of collapsible columns and airbags dramatically reduced driver fatalities.
